I agree that it's not completely a fair comparison. But here's why I think that:

With AI, you can offload almost everything. With the saw, all I'm offloading is the cutting.

I don't actually have to make any decisions when doing woodworking. I can just buy some plans and follow them. The only time I need to make decisions is when I make something unique.

TBF, that's almost all the time for me.

But also TBF, it's the same with AI.

Sure, I can let it make all the decisions, but then I'm not going to end up with something uniquely mine. It's going to keep pulling back towards its training. To get what I want, I need to keep course-correcting the AI while building.

Some people are going to be fine with that, and will let is just make whatever it wants, and call it good enough. That's just like buying the plans and following them blindly.

The difference between tablesaws and AI is, like I said above, the range of things it can do. It's like having all the saws I listed above, plus electric screw drivers, drills, laser levels, and the whole rest of the toolkit, all in 1 box. You even get a chatbot that will tell all those things what to do to follow the plans.

Making good plans has always been one of the hardest parts of both woodworking and software development.

When you have half-arsed plans (in either discipline) you need to fix things up as you go, and that hasn't changed with AI.

AI removed a lot of the other hard things, but left the hard planning step, and the hard "hide the screwups" steps.
For the simple reason that LLMs don't automate away any of those jobs. If they did, they'd sell you a "Data Scientist Pro Max 2000" subscription.

> You can't authenticate a person using their (public) fingerprint information.

Yes, but it's a signal! There's a cost to spoof it. A scammer could cheaply start a VM that clones your font profile, but at what cost could they replicate your CPU SKU and GPU combination to provide identical webGL timings?

Other signals include the ability of your employee to show their face on a video call, to sound like themselves on a voice call, the ability contact you from their home IP, to receive official mail at their listed address, to produce a second 2FA token you'd previously registered (but not activated) or repeat a code word you'd exchanged. Any of these things can be spoofed, bypassed, copied, or burgled, but each one imposes some cost on the attacker.

The question is how to surface this information in a way that equips help desk staff and doesn't deceive them into authorizing unnecessary risks.
